sn3.11:1.1: The prose with different verses is at [ud6.2]().
sn3.11:2.1: “Matted-hair ascetics” (_jaṭilā_) were Vedic ascetics practicing bathing and worshiping the sacred flame ([ud1.9]()). | “Jain ascetics” (_nigaṇṭhā_) were followers of Mahāvīra. | “Naked ascetics” (_acelakā_) were apparently also Brahmanical ([mn57]()), although several orders including Jains practiced nakedness. | Some (all?) “one-cloth ascetics” were Jains ([an6.57:4.1]()). | “Wanderers (_paribbājakā_) were homeless religious renunciates—male or female, Brahmanical or other—who wandered seeking alms. | For _khāri_ (“stuff”) see also [sn7.9:14.1]().
sn3.11:3.2: This sentence is phrased as a statement in all editions here, and in the parallel passage at [ud6.2:4.2]() all except the PTS edition, where it is a question. The commentary in both places confirms it is meant as a statement (_“ime arahanto”ti vutte_). Pasenadi is testing the Buddha.
sn3.11:7.1: The use of ascetics for spies, which is still common today, is detailed by Kauṭilya in his Arthaśāstra. Those seeking a job can imitate bald (_muṇḍa_) or matted-hair (_jaṭila_) ascetics, pretending to live on a handful of grass but secretly eating what they like (as here). Other spies disguised as merchants then acclaim them to build reputation (as Pasenadi here). When people seek prophecies, he foretells that those loyal to the king shall prosper and those who oppose him will suffer. The king’s minister then ensures that such prophecies come true (1.11.13, 1.13.15). Ascetic spies are taught to manipulate loyalties with morality tales (1.14) and to fool kings by faking magical powers (13.2). Princes may also don the guise of such ascetics in order to escape a coup (7.17.50).
